This is my very basic understanding of how nutrients work: If you work out a lot, you also need to eat a lot. If you work out a little you only need to eat a little. (And of course, you need a balanced diet with carbs, protein, fats etc)

My very basic understanding of protein powder is that powder is used by people who work out so much that they need to supplement their diet with protein powder, because it would be unreasonable for them to be able to eat so much protein without it.

No. Your basic assumption is wrong. You can get enough protein without powder. The issue is amount of calories consumed to get that amount of protein. And that depends on your metabolism. Everything is a matter of balance. But if you are working out really hard and ripping and building muscles,at least with me, it is possible to about feel when I'm not getting enough protein. Feels like my body is screaming for meat. Depending on my BMI when this happens, I either just eat more protein foods and/or add powder.

That said, a good protein powder/insulin boost post workout does seem to speed building muscle mass.

There are a lot of variables, so there isn't an exact rule. Just figure out what works best for you. And all the powder and creatine in the world won't do much if your regimen isn't going past what your basic diet supplies. I suggest experimenting to see what mix works for you. Genetics has a significant component as well. Overdosing protein you don't need just puts an extra load on your kidneys, same as overdosing vitamins.

Of course, if weight loss/lowering BMI is a goal along with building muscle, when I've been doing that, my diet trends towards mostly powder/supplements, minimum carbs. All depends on your exact circumstances.

Best of luck.

You need to calculate your daily macros. How much protein, fat, and carbs you need for how much energy your exerting. The formulas have been tweeked for more precision in the past couple years but for a while it was pretty standard that you wanted half your body weight for protein and fats and 1:1 for carbs. So if you weighed 150lbs you'd need about 75g of protein and fats and 150g of carbs.

Protein powder is a means of giving you additional protein without adding a ton of fats and carbs too. If you're able to meet all of your nutrient goals for the day without a protein shake you never need one. My brother is a powerlifter who's currently ~250lbs and has remarkable PRs, He's well over his 1600 total goal for squat deadlift and bench and he bulks on around 5500 calories or so. Okay we need to talk about a few things first. Your diet (as in what you eat) really has nothing to do with your workout. It's how much surplus food you eat that makes a difference. By default (regardless if you workout or not) you should be eating 40% Protein, 40% Carbs, and 20% Fats (refereed to as your marco spread). Carbs like oats and sweet potatoes, and fats like avocado and nuts. When you workout you need more more food (more calories) to grow muscle, but you still eat your macro spread. So you eat more calories in total (about ~250 more per day) with the same marco spread. Like wise to lose weight you eat ~500 less per day with the same macro spread.

Protein powder is just a quick easy to go to protein source. You literally do not need to use protein powder if you eat enough protein in your diet now. For me I need ~180 grams of protein. If chicken breast (skinless) is ~26g of protein, I would need to eat ~7 chicken breasts a day. That is kinda hard to do so I opt for a shake or two reduce how much chicken I need to eat, per day. Of course chicken isn't my only protein source, this is just to help illustrate the point. Note I'm on bulk right now, so my intake will most likely be hire than yours.

TL:DR as long as you can eat 40% protein in your daily diet, you don't need protein powder.
